title: Security & Compliance Program: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Compliance Evidence, and Risk
author: Lena Brooks
body:
Overview

This document is the canonical Security & Compliance Program overview for Redwood Inference covering role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, our Secure SDLC, incident response procedures for security events, compliance evidence workflows, and risk & exceptions handling. It is intended for engineers, product managers, SREs, and compliance stakeholders.

Goals
- Ensure least-privilege access to production and customer-sensitive systems.
- Provide reliable, tamper-evident audit logs to satisfy internal investigations and external audits.
- Maintain clear data residency and retention policies aligned to customer requirements and regulations.
- Embed security controls into the SDLC to reduce vulnerabilities and speed secure releases.
- Define repeatable incident response and evidence collection procedures for security incidents.
- Create a pragmatic risk and exceptions process to balance delivery with security posture.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Scope and Principles
- Applies to all Redwood-controlled systems: control plane services, console, internal tooling, CI/CD, and customer-facing admin consoles.
- Principle of least privilege: default deny, allow as required.
- Segregation of duties for production-access roles (developers vs. oncall vs. platform engineers).

Roles and Permissions (summary table)
| Role | Typical members | Scope | Privileges | Approval owner |
| Admin | Security leads, infra engineers | Organization-wide | Full access to IAM, billing, cloud accounts | Security Director |
| Platform Operator | SRE/Infra | Runtime clusters & autoscaling | Deploy, rollback, view logs | Eng-SRE Manager |
| Developer | Product & infra engineers | Non-prod, dev namespaces | Create/dev deploys, debug | Team Lead |
| Oncall | Pager duty engineers | Production incidents | Escalate, limited deploys, runbooks | Oncall Lead |

Key Controls
- Central Identity Provider: Redwood uses SSO via Okta (SAML + OIDC) for all employee access.
- MFA required for all interactive access and service token provisioning.
- Short-lived credentials: production service tokens and session credentials expire ≤ 12 hours by default; long-lived keys require approval and rotation plan.
- Attribute-based access: assign roles by team and environment tags, not individuals.
- Approval workflows: role elevation requests pass through approver (security/manager) and are time-boxed.

Procedures
1. Request access: Engineer opens an access request in Access Portal with justification and scope.
2. Manager approval: Team lead approves for business need.
3. Security review: Security team verifies least-privilege mapping and sets duration.
4. Grant: IAM system issues temporary role; all grants recorded in access log.
5. Revoke: Expired automatically or manually revoked after purpose completed.

Auditability
- All role grants and elevation requests are recorded in the Access Portal; logs forwarded to Audit Logging service (see section 2).

2) Audit Logging

Overview
- Purpose: Provide tamper-evident, searchable records for authentication, authorization, configuration changes, data access events, and system telemetry required for incident response and compliance evidence.

Log Sources
- Identity & Access (SSO, token issuance, role changes)
- Control Plane (deploys, model rollouts, routing changes)
- Runtime (model inference requests metadata, configuration changes)
- Data Access (customer data exports, KMS operations, key usage)
- System & Security (auth failures, privilege escalations, suspicious API patterns)

Retention & Storage
- All audit logs are ingested into a centralized logging cluster with WORM policies for restricted retention buckets.
- Default retention: 1 year in hot index, 3 years in cold storage for internal audit; extended retention per customer contractual obligations.
- Retention for regulated customers can be configured by region and contract.

Integrity and Monitoring
- Logs are forwarded over TLS, signed by edge collectors, and checksum-validated on ingest.
- Periodic integrity scans validate checksums; anomalies generate tickets to Security Ops.
- Alerts: predefined alerts for suspicious patterns (mass privilege grants, repeated auth failures, log deletion attempts).

Access and Queries
- Audit read access limited to security engineers, compliance owners, and approved auditors.
- Query playbooks exist for common investigations: user activity, service token usage, model inference sampling.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Policy Principles
- Customers choose the geographic region for data residency for stored customer data and persistent logs.
- Minimal data retention by default; store only what is required to operate the service and meet contractual obligations.

Data Classification
- Customer PII: must follow customer-specified residency.
- Control plane metadata (non-customer sensitive): default US/EU depending on deployment.
- Audit logs: stored in region aligned with customer contract; cross-region replication only with explicit consent.

Retention Baselines
- Short-term: ephemeral telemetry and trace details kept for 14–30 days in hot storage for debugging.
- Audit logs: 1–3 years depending on tier and contract.
- Backups: encrypted snapshots retained per backup policy table below.

Retention Table
| Data type | Default retention | Compliance options | Owner |
| Customer data (production) | As specified by customer (default 90 days) | 30 days — indefinite per contract | Product/Legal |
| Audit logs | 1 year hot / 3 years cold | Extended on contract per region | Security |
| Backups (DB snapshots) | 90 days | Archived longer on request | Eng-Infra |

Data Deletion Procedure (customer-requested)
1. Verify scope: Product verifies dataset and residency constraints.
2. Schedule deletion: Coordinate with infra for safe deletion window.
3. Delete & purge: Delete data from primary stores and initiate purge of backups; record actions in audit log.
4. Confirm: Send confirmation to customer and log the confirmation in compliance evidence store.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Software Development Lifecycle)

Philosophy
- Security is integrated into every phase: design, implementation, code review, testing, release, and post-deploy monitoring.

Key Practices
- Threat modeling: Required for new services and major features; maintain a threat model artifact in the design spec.
- Secure design checklist: cryptography, secrets management, least-privilege, fail-safe defaults.
- Static Analysis: PRs run SAST and dependency scanning; high and critical findings fail the build.
- Dynamic/Runtime Testing: Pre-prod runs DAST and fuzzing for public endpoints.
- Secret scanning: Blocked in CI; secrets policy auto-remediation steps.
- Dependency policy: Automatic patching for critical libs; dependency risk exceptions require security approval.

Release Controls
- Canary rollouts for model and control-plane changes with automatic rollback on error budget breach.
- Mandatory security checklist sign-off before production deploys for high-impact features.

Developer Support
- Security playbooks and guardrails published in eng-developer-experience.
- Regular training: secure coding workshops, quarterly capture-the-flag exercises.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Scope
- Covers security incidents impacting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of Redwood or customer data.

Incident Phases and Responsibilities
1. Detection & Triage (Owner: Oncall/Ops)
- Use alerts from Audit Logging, IDS, runtime monitors.
- Triage severity per incident taxonomy (P0–P3) using the security incident matrix.
2. Containment (Owner: Incident Commander)
- Short-term containment actions: revoke credentials, isolate nodes, disable compromised services.
- Document containment steps in the incident timeline.
3. Eradication & Remediation (Owner: Security Engineering)
- Root cause analysis, patching, configuration hardening, and verification in staging.
4. Recovery (Owner: Platform)
- Gradual restore with monitoring and validation; avoid full data restores without validation.
5. Post-incident Review (Owner: Security & Eng)
- Produce a Postmortem with actions, owners, and due dates. Security issues feed into Secure SDLC improvements.

Evidence Collection Checklist
- Preserve audit logs (WORM) and snapshot relevant systems immediately.
- Export SSO/access logs, token issuance history, and relevant cloud provider audit logs.
- Hash and store evidence artifacts in Compliance Evidence Store.

Communications
- Security handles initial internal comms; Customer Success and Legal own customer notifications per contractual SLA.
- Public disclosures coordinated with PR and Legal.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose
- Provide reproducible artifacts for SOC2, ISO, and customer audits.

Artifacts and Owners (table)
| Artifact | Typical contents | Owner | Retention |
| Access request history | Requester, approver, justification, duration | Security | 3 years |
| Audit log exports | Signed logs for period | Security | As per contract |
| Policies & procedures | Versioned docs, review history | Legal/Security | Indefinite |
| Configuration snapshots | Infrastructure state at time | Eng-Infra | 3 years |

Evidence Request Procedure
1. Auditor request: Request logged in Compliance Tracker.
2. Scope & timeframe: Security & Legal define scope.
3. Artifact collection: Security exports signed logs and config snapshots.
4. Review: Internal review before release to auditor.
5. Delivery: Secure transmission (SFTP or portal) and receipt confirmation recorded.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process

Risk Assessment
- All exceptions start with a Risk Assessment: threat, likelihood, impact, compensating controls, and mitigation timeline.

Exception Workflow
1. Submit exception request in Risk Portal with technical rationale and duration.
2. Security review: Evaluate risk score and required compensating controls.
3. Approvals: Low-risk exceptions may be approved by Security Manager; high-risk require Security Director and CTO sign-off.
4. Monitoring: Exceptions tracked with expiration dates and monitoring hooks.

Example: Dependency Upgrade Delay
- Risk: Known vuln in non-critical test-only dependency.
- Compensating controls: Network isolation for CI runners, limited artifact access, deadline for upgrade (30 days).
- Approval: Security Manager documented in Risk Portal.

8) Roles and Ownership Summary
- Security: overall program owner, audit log integrity, incident response lead, evidence collection.
- Eng-Infra: implement RBAC controls, backups, retention enforcements.
- Eng-SRE: monitoring, alerting, runbooks, and canary rollback controls.
- Product & Legal: contractual requirements for residency and retention, customer communications.

10) Maintenance and Review Cadence
- Policy review: annually or on major product changes.
- Audit log integrity checks: daily.
- Incident drill: quarterly table-top; annual full game-day.
- Evidence readiness audit: quarterly prior to audits.

Appendix A: Quick Runbooks
- Grant elevated access (emergency)
  1. Team lead files emergency request and tags urgency in Access Portal.
  2. Security oncall phone approves and assigns 24h window.
  3. Actions taken must be logged and a post-approval review is required within 72 hours.

- Preserve evidence after suspected compromise
  1. Isolate affected instances.
  2. Trigger export of audit logs for the last 30 days to Compliance Evidence Store.
  3. Create a forensic snapshot and hash; store hash and artifact in immutable storage.
